title: Aachen surrenders
body:
For the first time in the war, a German city fell to the Allies.

21 October 1944. After five and a half weeks of fighting, the last German garrison in Aachen, holed up in the Hotel Quellenhof, finally surrendered.

Aachen had little military value. What it had was meaning. It was the old capital of Charlemagne, and Nazi propaganda held him up as the founder of Germany's first empire. Hitler ordered the city held at all costs.

The U.S. 1st and 30th Infantry Divisions closed the ring around it, then fought through the ruins house by house, sometimes blasting through walls rather than stepping into the streets. American losses passed 7,000. About 5,600 Germans went into captivity, many marching past the wreckage of the city they had been told to defend.

The road into Germany was open, but it would not be easy.
photoNote: German prisoners taken at the fall of Aachen marching through the ruined streets, October 1944. NARA 541597, public domain.
threads:
For the first time in the war, a German city fell to the Allies.

21 October 1944. After five and a half weeks of fighting, the last defenders of Aachen surrendered in the ruins of the Hotel Quellenhof.

It was Charlemagne's old capital, and Hitler wanted it held at all costs. The U.S. 1st and 30th Infantry Divisions took it house by house.

video.note: AACHEN, GERMANY, 15 October 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2654 (NARA 16458), cameraman Sgt. Newman, silent. An M-10 tank destroyer fires point blank into a building, infantry climb over a wall between houses, and a crew pushes a 57mm antitank gun through the streets. Filmed during the battle, six days before the surrender. U.S. government work, public domain (NARA's blanket 'possibly copyright' flag on Signal Corps reels, as on Leyte's 111-ADC-3205). Clip uses 1:42.0 to 1:47.6, 4:18.5 to 4:23.5, and 5:45.3 to 5:50.3.

declassified.fact: The Americans picked Franz Oppenhoff, recommended by Aachen's bishop, as the city's new mayor. Hitler demanded the 'treasonous puppet' be eliminated, and an SS team was flown in aboard a captured American bomber. On the night of 25 March 1945 one of them shot Oppenhoff dead at his home.
